data.name: Borstal
data.detailed_description:
Survival roguelike novellas with meaningful choices and multiple endings!

There are two scenarios currently: first one is set on a small island. It's 1926, you're 13 years old and it is raining. You're looking for your lost father.

The second scenario puts you in the role of a mountaineer trying to climb an eight-thousander.

It's a coffee-break game, randomized every playthrough - especially if you like to die a lot during your coffee breaks.

reviews.review:
Borstal is an unusual blend of genres that feels like a forgotten interactive paperback brought to life. Developed and published by The Secret Pie, the game combines survival mechanics, procedural generation, and narrative-driven decision-making into a compact package that is more interested in tension and atmosphere than flashy presentation. Released during a period when survival games were largely focused on crafting and open worlds, Borstal instead takes a minimalist approach, asking players to survive through careful choices and adaptability. It presents itself as a collection of short survival stories, each designed to be replayed multiple times, and while its ambitions occasionally exceed its scope, there is a distinct identity here that separates it from more conventional indie releases.

The game features two separate adventures, each centered around an isolated struggle against nature. The first follows a young boy in 1926 who becomes stranded on a mysterious island while searching for his missing father. The second shifts to the role of a climber attempting to survive the ascent of a towering mountain. Both scenarios emphasize vulnerability and uncertainty, making every action feel significant. Supplies are limited, hazards are unpredictable, and survival often depends on weighing immediate needs against long-term consequences. The stories themselves are intentionally understated, revealing details gradually through exploration and player actions rather than lengthy dialogue sequences.

What makes Borstal particularly interesting is its use of procedural elements. No two journeys play out exactly the same way, as item placements, encounters, and environmental circumstances can change between sessions. This design choice adds longevity to a game that can otherwise be completed relatively quickly. Players are encouraged to experiment with different decisions, uncover alternate endings, and learn from previous failures. The roguelike influence is evident throughout, especially in the way the game embraces repetition as part of the experience. Losing progress is not treated as punishment but as another chapter in understanding how to survive the world that Borstal presents.

Gameplay is deliberately simple, relying on exploration, inventory management, and strategic planning rather than complex systems. This accessibility works in the game's favor, making it easy to pick up and enjoy in shorter sessions. At the same time, the streamlined mechanics can feel limiting. There are moments when players may wish for deeper interactions or additional content to flesh out the game's ideas. The interface is functional but occasionally rough around the edges, and the minimalist visuals, while effective in establishing mood, will not appeal to everyone. Nevertheless, the understated presentation complements the game's themes of isolation and perseverance remarkably well.

Atmosphere is where Borstal shines the brightest. The lonely island and the unforgiving mountain are both memorable settings despite their simplicity. There is a persistent sense of unease that accompanies each playthrough, heightened by the knowledge that a single poor decision can end an adventure prematurely. The game's soundtrack and environmental design work together to create an experience that feels contemplative rather than action-oriented. Instead of overwhelming players with objectives and markers, Borstal trusts them to immerse themselves in the moment and discover their own path forward.

Despite its strengths, Borstal is undeniably a niche experience. The limited number of scenarios means that some players will exhaust its content relatively quickly, and those expecting an expansive survival sandbox may come away disappointed. However, the game's concise nature is also part of its appeal. It respects the player's time, offering complete experiences that can be enjoyed over the course of an evening while still leaving room for replayability through alternate outcomes and randomized events.

Borstal succeeds because it commits fully to its concept. It is less a traditional survival game and more a pair of interactive novellas shaped by player choice. Its imperfections are easy to spot, but so is the creativity behind its design. The Secret Pie crafted a title that prioritizes mood, experimentation, and storytelling over scale, resulting in an experience that remains memorable years after its release. For players willing to embrace its minimalist philosophy and slower pace, Borstal offers an engaging and distinctive journey through two harsh but fascinating worlds.

Rating: 6/10
